## M1-E01

**Read the ER diagram** · SOURCE · question posed in the lecture  
Source: [lecture1 L167-210](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“So here, we have what's called a crow's foot notation”*

```sql
-- Model answer:
-- 1. Many-to-many: an author can write many books (Olga Tokarczuk wrote three here) and a book can have several authors.
-- 2. A book has ZERO to many translators (some aren't translated); a translator translated at least one book.
-- 3. One-to-many: one book, many ratings, so book_id is stored in ratings as a foreign key.
```

**Why:** These diagrams are how you communicate a design. Lecture 2 makes you draw your own (M2-E01).

## M1-E02

**Why not use the ISBN as the primary key?** · SOURCE · question posed in the lecture  
Source: [lecture1 L340-380](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“And we can actually construct our very own primary key.”*

```sql
-- Model answer:
-- 1. Size: as text it is ~17 bytes, repeated in every referencing row (e.g. thousands of ratings).
-- 2. Stored as a number instead, an ISBN that starts with 0 loses that 0, so it no longer identifies the book.
-- Alternative: a surrogate integer id (1, 2, 3 …) that is unique and never reused for another row.
--   books.id is then the PRIMARY key; ratings.book_id and authored.book_id are FOREIGN keys to it.
```

**Why:** "It doesn't quite matter what number we choose so long as this number uniquely identifies the book" (L367-369).

## M1-E09

**Join sea lions to their migrations** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture1 L1108-1162](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“So, this is our example, then, of an INNER JOIN.”*

```sql
SELECT * FROM "sea_lions"
JOIN "migrations" ON "migrations"."id" = "sea_lions"."id";
```

**Why:** A plain JOIN is an INNER JOIN. Jolee (no migration) and the two migrations of untracked sea lions disappear, because only matching rows survive.

## M1-E10

**Keep every tracked sea lion (LEFT JOIN)** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture1 L1224-1251](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“Where we left off Jolee earlier, we've now”*

```sql
SELECT * FROM "sea_lions"
LEFT JOIN "migrations" ON "migrations"."id" = "sea_lions"."id";
```

**Why:** Jolee's distance and days come back as NULL. RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of the right table instead (L1252-1272).

## M1-E11

**Keep everything (FULL JOIN)** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture1 L1274-1288](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“A FULL JOIN, though, allows us to see the entirety of both tables”*

```sql
SELECT * FROM "sea_lions"
FULL JOIN "migrations" ON "migrations"."id" = "sea_lions"."id";
```

**Why:** RIGHT and FULL JOIN need SQLite 3.39 (2022) or newer. Older versions report a syntax error.

## M1-E18

**Homework: in exactly one of the two sets** · SOURCE · explicitly left to the learner in the lecture  
Source: [lecture1 L1461-1466](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“I actually saved that one for you to do as homework”*

```sql
SELECT "name" FROM (
    SELECT "name" FROM "authors" EXCEPT SELECT "name" FROM "translators"
)
UNION
SELECT "name" FROM (
    SELECT "name" FROM "translators" EXCEPT SELECT "name" FROM "authors"
);
```

**Why:** Without the subqueries, chained set operators run left to right: `A EXCEPT T UNION T EXCEPT A` means `((A EXCEPT T) UNION T) EXCEPT A`, which is not the symmetric difference.
Equivalent: `(A UNION T) EXCEPT (A INTERSECT T)`.

## M1-E20

**Only the well-rated books (HAVING)** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture1 L1753-1770](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“SQL uses a different keyword for conditions on groups”*, [lecture1 L1811-1829](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“so great question here to re-implement much of what we did last time”*

## D1-01

**Joined on the wrong column** · GENERATED · written for this system (reinforces a concept from the source)  
Source: [lecture1 L1119-1132](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“I have to tell SQL which two columns to try to JOIN these tables by.”*, [lecture4 L207-219](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“linking it up by looking at the authors dot ID column”*

Broken version:
```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "authors"
JOIN "authored" ON "authors"."id" = "authored"."book_id"
JOIN "books" ON "books"."id" = "authored"."book_id"
WHERE "name" = 'Fernanda Melchor';
```

Fixed:
```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "authors"
JOIN "authored" ON "authors"."id" = "authored"."author_id"
JOIN "books" ON "books"."id" = "authored"."book_id"
WHERE "name" = 'Fernanda Melchor';
```

**Diagnosis (join):** The broken query matched author id 24 with **book** id 24, which is a coincidence of numbers, not a relationship.
Ids from different tables share values (lecture2 L310-326), so the database can't catch this. Only you can.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

| title |
|---|
| Paradais |
| Hurricane Season |

</details>

## D1-02

**Duplicate rows from a one-to-many join** · GENERATED · written for this system (reinforces a concept from the source)  
Source: [lecture1 L320-334](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“So this is an example of how we could represent”*

Broken version:
```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "books"
JOIN "ratings" ON "ratings"."book_id" = "books"."id"
WHERE "year" = 2022;
```

Fixed:
```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "books"
WHERE "year" = 2022
AND "id" IN (SELECT "book_id" FROM "ratings");
```

**Diagnosis (duplicates):** Joining to the "many" side of a one-to-many relationship multiplies rows.

## D1-03

**One average instead of one per book** · GENERATED · written for this system (reinforces a concept from the source)  
Source: [lecture1 L1683-1703](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“I'm getting the average of all of these ratings not grouped by book_id.”*

Broken version:
```sql
SELECT "book_id", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "rating" FROM "ratings";
```

Fixed:
```sql
SELECT "book_id", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "rating" FROM "ratings" GROUP BY "book_id";
```

**Diagnosis (aggregation):** SQLite even let you select the bare `book_id` next to the aggregate (it picks an arbitrary row's value). Most other DBMSs reject that query outright.

## D1-04

**`=` with a subquery that returns many rows** · GENERATED · written for this system (reinforces a concept from the source)  
Source: [lecture1 L969-984](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“if you're looking to see if some id is part of a list of ids”*

Broken version:
```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "movies" WHERE "id" = (
    SELECT "movie_id" FROM "stars" WHERE "person_id" = (
        SELECT "id" FROM "people" WHERE "name" = 'Tom Hanks'
    )
);
```

Fixed:
```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "movies" WHERE "id" IN (
    SELECT "movie_id" FROM "stars" WHERE "person_id" = (
        SELECT "id" FROM "people" WHERE "name" = 'Tom Hanks'
    )
);
```

**Diagnosis (subquery):** Use `IN` when a subquery can return several rows. `=` is fine for the innermost one, since there is one Tom Hanks.

|---|

## D1-07

**WHERE on an aggregate** · SOURCE · question posed in the lecture  
Source: [lecture1 L1755-1764](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“But I can't because these are now not individual rows.”*

Broken version:
```sql
SELECT "book_id", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "average rating"
FROM "ratings"
WHERE "average rating" > 4.0
GROUP BY "book_id";
```

Fixed:
```sql
SELECT "book_id", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "average rating"
FROM "ratings"
GROUP BY "book_id"
HAVING "average rating" > 4.0;
```

**Diagnosis (aggregation):** WHERE filters individual rows and HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

## D1-08

**LEFT JOIN wanted, INNER JOIN written** · GENERATED · written for this system (reinforces a concept from the source)  
Source: [lecture1 L1149-1162](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“well, let's sadly just get rid of the row.”*

Broken version:
```sql
SELECT "name", "distance" FROM "sea_lions"
JOIN "migrations" ON "migrations"."id" = "sea_lions"."id";
```

Fixed:
```sql
SELECT "name", "distance" FROM "sea_lions"
LEFT JOIN "migrations" ON "migrations"."id" = "sea_lions"."id";
```

**Diagnosis (join):** An INNER JOIN silently drops unmatched rows. Choose the join from the question ("every sea lion" means LEFT).

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

| name | distance |
|---|---|
| Ayah | 1000 |
| Spot | 1531 |
| Tiger | 1370 |
| Mabel | 1622 |
| Rick | 1491 |
| Jolee | NULL |

</details>

## D1-09

**UNION of mismatched columns** · SOURCE · question posed in the lecture  
Source: [lecture1 L1652-1662](../sources/lecture1.txt) *“you always have to have the same number”*

Broken version:
```sql
SELECT "id", "name" FROM "authors"
UNION
SELECT "name" FROM "translators";
```

Fixed:
```sql
SELECT "name" FROM "authors"
UNION
SELECT "name" FROM "translators";
```

**Diagnosis (syntax):** "SELECTs to the left and right of UNION do not have the same number of result columns". Both sides need the same number of columns, and they should hold the same kind of data (L1652-1662).
